 ECONOMY 
 Top court rejects extended tax deadlines
 Certain older cases must close once the standard 5-year limitation expires, absent lawful exceptions 
 [IntTme News] 
 Prokopis Hatzinikolaou 
 October 30, 2026 
 30.10.2026 • 09:15 
 The Council of State, Greece’s supreme administrative court, has imposed new limits on the government’s ability to assess taxes and penalties in older tax cases, ruling that extended limitation periods exceed constitutional boundaries.
 In decision 1246/2026, a seven-member panel of the court’s Second Chamber found unconstitutional a 10-year limitation period established under Law 4646/2019 for certain earlier tax periods. It also ruled invalid the provision allowing a 20-year limitation period in cases of tax evasion.
 The court said limitation periods must provide a reasonable, clearly defined timeframe for tax assessments, consistent with the constitutional principles of proportionality and legal certainty. The 20-year period went beyond what was necessary to detect tax violations, particularly given the tax administration’s access to electronic tools, modern auditing methods and risk-analysis systems.
 The ruling concerns the 2012 and 2013 financial years and tax years 2014 through 2017. Cases remaining open solely under the challenged 10-year provision will close if the standard five-year limitation period has expired and no other lawful exception applies.
 The dispute arose from a penalty imposed on a honey-producing sole proprietorship for receiving a fictitious invoice during 2013. The invoice had a net value of €11,600, and the penalty imposed in 2020 totaled €4,640, or 40% of the invoice’s value.
 Tax authorities issued the penalty on November 24, 2020, after the five-year limitation period had expired. The taxpayer’s administrative appeal was rejected, but the Administrative Court of First Instance in Kozani subsequently annulled the penalty, finding the transitional provision permitting the extended period invalid.
 The Independent Authority for Public Revenue appealed to the Council of State, arguing that the 2019 legislation had reduced the previously applicable 20-year period to 10 years, making the arrangement more favorable to taxpayers rather than extending the deadline.
 The Council of State rejected that interpretation and found the transitional provision contrary to Article 78, paragraphs 1 and 2, of the Constitution.
 In the specific case, the court also noted that tax authorities had not cited supplementary evidence that could justify different treatment. It therefore concluded that the government’s right to impose the penalty had expired on December 31, 2019.
